Title: A Combined Pore Blockage and Cake Filtration Model for Protein Fouling during Microfiltration

Abstract: Previous studies of protein fouling during microfiltration have shown significant discrepancies between filtrate flux data and predictions of the classical pore blockage, pore constriction, and cake filtration models. A new mathematical model was developed for the filtrate flux which accounts for initial fouling due to pore blockage and subsequent fouling due to the growth of a protein cake or deposit over these initially blocked regions. The model explicitly accounts for the inhomogeneity in the cake layer thickness over different regions of the membrane arising from the time-dependent blockage of the pore surface. The model was shown to be in excellent agreement with experimental data obtained during the stirred cell filtration of bovine serum albumin solutions through polycarbonate track-etched microfiltration membranes over the entire course of the filtration. The model provides a smooth transition from the pore blockage to cake filtration regimes, eliminating the need to use different mathematical formulations to describe these two phenomena. In addition, the model provides the first quantitative explanation for some of the unusual observations reported previously in investigations of protein microfiltration. The results provide important insights into the underlying mechanisms of protein fouling during microfiltration. © 2000 Academic Press

Model: Combined pore blockage and cake filtration model
Laws:
(4) [definition] Total filtrate flow through the fouled membrane is the sum of the flows through open and blocked pores.
(5) [constitutive] Flow through open pores is given by a Darcy‑like relation using the clean membrane resistance.
(6) [constitutive] Flow through blocked pores is obtained by integrating the local resistance over the blocked area.
(7) [balance] Open membrane area decreases at a rate proportional to the convective protein‑aggregate flow to the surface.
(8) [constitutive] Pore blockage parameter α equals the area blocked per unit mass of a protein aggregate.
(10) [balance] Mass of protein deposit per unit area grows proportionally to the convective transport of protein through the blocked region.
(11) [constitutive] Filtrate flux through a blocked region is given by pressure drop divided by viscosity times the sum of clean membrane and deposit resistances.
(12) [balance] Hydraulic resistance of the protein deposit increases proportionally to the increase in deposit mass per area.

States (computed by the ODEs):
- A_{open}: area of membrane that remains uncovered at any given time
- m_{p}: mass of the protein deposit per unit area
- R_{p}: hydraulic resistance of the protein deposit over a particular region of the membrane

Inputs (variables no law computes):
- \Delta P: transmembrane pressure driving filtration
- A_{blocked}: area of membrane surface blocked by protein aggregates
- C_{b}: bulk protein concentration
- f: fractional amount of total protein present as aggregates
- A_{agg}: membrane area blocked by a single aggregate
- M_{agg}: mass of a single aggregate
- f^{\prime}: fraction of the proteins that contribute to the growth of the deposit
- R^{\prime}: proportionality constant linking hydraulic resistance of the protein deposit to its mass per unit area

Model-wide assumptions:
- The initial deposit is partially permeable, allowing finite flow through blocked pores.
- Pore coverage rate is proportional to convective protein‑aggregate flow rate.
- Deposit hydraulic resistance is directly proportional to mass per unit area.
- Specific protein layer resistance R' is constant during constant‑pressure filtration.

answer.description: The model describes the fouling of a polycarbonate track‑etched microfiltration membrane by bovine serum albumin during constant‑pressure stirred‑cell experiments. It predicts the time‑dependent filtrate flux by coupling two mechanisms: (i) pore blockage, where protein aggregates cover open pores and still allow flow through a combined membrane‑plus‑deposit resistance, and (ii) cake formation, where the deposited protein mass grows and adds hydraulic resistance. The governing ODEs track the open membrane area, deposit mass per unit area, and deposit resistance, providing a smooth transition between the blockage and cake regimes without switching mathematical formulations.
